name: Unemployment rate
definition: The share of the labour force without work but available for and seeking employment, using modelled International Labour Organization estimates.
interpretation: Lower values generally mean a larger share of people seeking work can find it, but very low rates can coexist with weak job quality or low participation.
whyItMatters: Unemployment is a central signal of whether an economy is translating activity into accessible paid work.
caveat: It excludes people outside the labour force and does not describe wages, hours, informality, job security, or discouraged workers.

name: Female unemployment rate
definition: The share of the female labour force without work but available for and seeking employment, using modelled ILO estimates.
interpretation: Compare this rate with the male rate and female labour-force participation to understand gender differences in access to work.
whyItMatters: Gender differences in unemployment can reveal unequal access to jobs, occupational segregation, discrimination, and care constraints.
caveat: Women who are not counted in the labour force are outside the denominator, so unemployment alone can understate labour-market exclusion.

name: Male unemployment rate
definition: The share of the male labour force without work but available for and seeking employment, using modelled ILO estimates.
interpretation: Compare this rate with the female rate and male labour-force participation rather than reading it as a complete measure of work conditions.
whyItMatters: The measure provides the corresponding male benchmark needed to interpret gender differences in labour-market access.
caveat: It excludes men outside the labour force and does not measure pay, job quality, informality, underemployment, or hours worked.

name: Youth unemployment rate
definition: The share of the labour force ages 15–24 without work but available for and seeking employment, using modelled ILO estimates.
interpretation: Higher values signal greater difficulty for young people who are participating in the labour market to find work.
whyItMatters: Early exclusion from work can have lasting effects on income, skills, independence, and confidence in institutions.
caveat: Students and other young people outside the labour force are excluded; use the NEET rate alongside this measure.

name: Female youth unemployment rate
definition: The share of the female labour force ages 15–24 without work but available for and seeking employment, using modelled ILO estimates.
interpretation: Read it beside male youth unemployment and the NEET rate to identify gendered barriers during the school-to-work transition.
whyItMatters: Young women can face compounded barriers linked to gender, age, care responsibilities, mobility, and occupational segregation.
caveat: The denominator excludes young women outside the labour force and therefore does not capture every form of economic exclusion.

name: Male youth unemployment rate
definition: The share of the male labour force ages 15–24 without work but available for and seeking employment, using modelled ILO estimates.
interpretation: Compare it with the corresponding female rate and the total youth rate to see how unemployment differs by gender.
whyItMatters: The male rate provides an essential comparison for assessing whether youth labour-market barriers are gendered.
caveat: It excludes young men outside the labour force and does not measure job quality, informality, or underemployment.

name: Youth not in employment, education or training
definition: The share of young people who are neither employed nor participating in education or training.
interpretation: Lower values indicate that more young people are connected to work, education, or skills development.
whyItMatters: NEET status captures disconnection that ordinary unemployment rates miss because it includes people outside the labour force.
caveat: Age ranges and survey treatment can vary, and the measure does not distinguish voluntary breaks from constrained exclusion.

name: Female labour-force participation
definition: The proportion of women ages 15 and older who are working or actively seeking work, using modelled ILO estimates.
interpretation: Compare it with the male rate and local education, retirement, care, and labour-market conditions rather than assuming higher is always better.
whyItMatters: Participation reflects women’s access to paid work and the constraints created by care, norms, safety, and job availability.
caveat: Participation does not indicate job quality or pay and can rise because households face hardship rather than improved opportunity.

name: Male labour-force participation
definition: The proportion of men ages 15 and older who are working or actively seeking work, using modelled ILO estimates.
interpretation: Use it as the comparison required to understand gender gaps in labour-force participation and access to paid work.
whyItMatters: The male benchmark helps separate general labour-market weakness from gender-specific barriers affecting women.
caveat: Participation does not indicate job quality, pay, informality, underemployment, or whether non-participation is voluntary.

name: Primary school completion rate
definition: The number of new entrants to the last grade of primary education divided by the population at the intended graduation age.
interpretation: Higher values generally indicate that more children persist through the end of primary education.
whyItMatters: Completion is a stronger access measure than enrolment alone because it captures progression through the primary cycle.
caveat: Values can exceed 100 because of over-age or under-age pupils, repetition, migration, and population-estimate differences.

name: Children out of primary school
definition: The share of children of official primary-school age who are not enrolled in primary or secondary education.
interpretation: Lower values indicate broader access to formal schooling among children of primary-school age.
whyItMatters: Exclusion from primary education is an early warning of barriers linked to poverty, conflict, disability, gender, or geography.
caveat: Administrative and population data may differ, and enrolment does not ensure attendance, learning, safety, or completion.

name: Secondary school enrolment
definition: Total secondary enrolment, regardless of age, divided by the population of the official secondary-school age group.
interpretation: Higher values usually indicate wider participation, but gross ratios can exceed 100 when pupils are outside the official age range.
whyItMatters: Secondary education expands foundational skills, future study options, employment pathways, health knowledge, and civic participation.
caveat: The gross ratio is not the percentage of appropriately aged children enrolled and does not measure attendance, completion, or learning.

name: Tertiary education enrolment
definition: Total tertiary enrolment, regardless of age, divided by the population in the five-year age group following secondary-school completion.
interpretation: Higher values indicate broader tertiary participation but do not reveal programme quality, completion, affordability, or labour-market fit.
whyItMatters: Access to tertiary education shapes advanced skills, professional capacity, research, mobility, and distribution of opportunity.
caveat: Gross ratios can exceed 100 and are sensitive to international students, older learners, programme length, and population estimates.

name: Adult literacy rate
definition: The percentage of people ages 15 and older who can read and write a short, simple statement about everyday life with understanding.
interpretation: Higher values indicate wider basic literacy, though the threshold does not capture the full range of reading and writing proficiency.
whyItMatters: Literacy affects access to information, services, work, political participation, health knowledge, and further learning.
caveat: Assessment and self-report methods differ, data can be infrequent, and a binary literacy threshold hides proficiency differences.

name: Learning poverty
definition: The estimated share of children at late-primary age who cannot read and understand a simple text, adjusted for children who are out of school.
interpretation: Lower values mean more children reach minimum reading proficiency by the end of primary-school age.
whyItMatters: It links access and learning, revealing whether schooling translates into a foundational capability needed for later education.
caveat: Estimates combine assessments and out-of-school data from different years and methods; coverage and uncertainty vary substantially.

name: Maternal mortality ratio
definition: The estimated number of women who die from pregnancy-related causes while pregnant or within 42 days of termination, per 100,000 live births.
interpretation: Lower values indicate safer pregnancy and childbirth conditions and stronger access to timely, effective maternal care.
whyItMatters: Maternal deaths are highly sensitive to health-system access, reproductive autonomy, poverty, transport, and quality of care.
caveat: This is a modelled estimate because registration is incomplete in many countries; uncertainty intervals are not displayed here.

name: Universal health coverage service index
definition: An index of coverage of essential health services spanning reproductive, maternal, newborn, child, infectious-disease, and noncommunicable-disease services and service capacity.
interpretation: Higher scores indicate broader average coverage of the tracer services included in the index.
whyItMatters: The measure gives a system-level view of whether people can obtain a broad package of essential health services.
caveat: It is a composite of tracer indicators, not a direct measure of every service, care quality, equity, or protection from health costs.

name: DPT immunisation coverage
definition: The percentage of children ages 12–23 months who received the recommended DPT vaccinations protecting against diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus.
interpretation: Higher values indicate broader routine childhood immunisation coverage and reach of primary health services.
whyItMatters: Vaccination prevents avoidable illness and death and is a practical signal of basic health-system reach.
caveat: Administrative reports and surveys can disagree, national averages hide local gaps, and the measure covers only one vaccine series.

name: Poverty below $3.00 a day
definition: The percentage of the population living below $3.00 per person per day in 2021 purchasing-power-parity international dollars.
interpretation: Lower values mean fewer people live below this global extreme-poverty threshold.
whyItMatters: The indicator provides a common international floor for tracking severe material deprivation across countries and time.
caveat: Household surveys are intermittent and methods differ; the global line does not replace national poverty measures or show poverty depth.

name: Multidimensional poverty headcount
definition: The share of people identified as multidimensionally poor under the UNDP and Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative global methodology.
interpretation: Lower values indicate fewer people experience overlapping deprivations across health, education, and living standards.
whyItMatters: Income alone can miss simultaneous disadvantages that shape whether people can live healthy, educated, and secure lives.
caveat: Survey years and indicators vary by country, many countries lack estimates, and values are not necessarily from the same reference year.

name: Women in national parliaments
definition: The share of seats held by women in single or lower chambers of national parliaments at the reference date.
interpretation: Higher values indicate more balanced descriptive representation, with parity at approximately 50 percent.
whyItMatters: Political representation affects whose experiences and priorities are present in national decision-making institutions.
caveat: Seat share does not measure political power, intersectional representation, policy influence, electoral fairness, or conditions outside parliament.

name: Adolescent fertility rate
definition: The annual number of births to women ages 15–19 per 1,000 women in that age group.
interpretation: Lower values generally indicate fewer adolescent births and often reflect greater reproductive choice and access to education and health services.
whyItMatters: Early childbearing is associated with health risks and can constrain education, income, and autonomy, though circumstances differ.
caveat: The rate does not distinguish wanted from unwanted births and should not be used to stigmatise adolescents or parents.

name: Human Development Index
definition: A composite index of achievement in a long and healthy life, knowledge, and a decent standard of living.
interpretation: Higher values indicate greater average achievement across the three dimensions, but do not show how achievements are distributed.
whyItMatters: HDI broadens assessment beyond economic output by combining health, education, and material living standards.
caveat: It compresses complex systems into one number and is recalculated across the full time series when methods or source data change.

name: Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index
definition: The Human Development Index adjusted downward for inequality in the distribution of health, education, and income achievements.
interpretation: The value approaches HDI when achievements are evenly distributed and falls further below HDI as inequality increases.
whyItMatters: It connects average human development with distribution, showing how much achievement is effectively lost to inequality.
caveat: Data availability is narrower than HDI, and the index still cannot describe which groups experience each disadvantage.

name: Gender Inequality Index
definition: A composite index of gender inequality in reproductive health, empowerment, and labour-market participation.
interpretation: Lower values indicate less inequality between women and men across the dimensions included in the index.
whyItMatters: It summarizes several structural gender disadvantages that cannot be understood from any single outcome alone.
caveat: The index is not a complete measure of gender equality and excludes gender diversity, violence, unpaid care, laws, and many lived experiences.

name: Gender Development Index
definition: The ratio of female to male Human Development Index values across health, education, and estimated earned income.
interpretation: A value near 1 indicates approximate parity; values below or above 1 indicate a gap in one direction and should be read with component data.
whyItMatters: It provides a direct gender comparison in basic human-development achievements rather than only reporting national averages.
caveat: Parity can occur at low achievement levels, the ratio can hide offsetting gaps, and earned-income estimates involve modelling assumptions.

name: Planetary pressures-adjusted HDI
definition: The Human Development Index adjusted for a country’s carbon-dioxide emissions per person and material footprint per person.
interpretation: The score falls below HDI when human-development achievements are associated with greater planetary pressures.
whyItMatters: It asks whether high human development is being achieved within a more environmentally sustainable resource and emissions profile.
caveat: It covers two environmental pressures, not ecological sustainability as a whole, and inherits the limitations of HDI and footprint estimates.

name: Safely managed drinking water
definition: The share of people using an improved drinking-water source that is accessible on premises, available when needed, and free from priority contamination.
interpretation: Higher values indicate broader access to drinking water that meets the safely managed service standard.
whyItMatters: Safe and reliable water is foundational to health, dignity, education, care work, and economic participation.
caveat: National estimates may combine surveys and modelling and can conceal large rural, urban, regional, income, and racialized inequalities.

name: Safely managed sanitation
definition: The share of people using an improved sanitation facility that is not shared and whose waste is safely disposed of in situ or treated off site.
interpretation: Higher values indicate broader access to sanitation that safely manages human waste.
whyItMatters: Safe sanitation protects health, dignity, safety, water quality, school attendance, and environmental conditions.
caveat: National estimates may combine surveys and modelling and do not necessarily describe service reliability, affordability, or local inequalities.

name: Access to clean cooking fuels and technologies
definition: The share of the population primarily using fuels and technologies classified as clean for cooking under international health guidance.
interpretation: Higher values indicate less reliance on polluting household cooking fuels and technologies.
whyItMatters: Clean cooking reduces household air pollution, health risks, fuel collection burdens, and associated gendered time costs.
caveat: Primary-fuel classification can miss households that stack multiple fuels and does not fully capture affordability or reliable access.

name: Intentional homicide rate
definition: The number of unlawful deaths purposefully inflicted on a person by another person per 100,000 population.
interpretation: Lower values generally indicate a lower level of lethal interpersonal violence.
whyItMatters: Lethal violence directly affects life, freedom, trust, mobility, economic activity, and the legitimacy of public institutions.
caveat: Recording practices, criminal-justice capacity, conflict classification, and missing cases affect comparability and timeliness.

name: Greenhouse-gas emissions per capita
definition: Total territorial greenhouse-gas emissions excluding land use, land-use change, and forestry, divided by population and expressed as carbon-dioxide equivalent.
interpretation: Lower values indicate fewer territorial greenhouse-gas emissions per resident, though development needs and historical responsibility differ.
whyItMatters: Per-person emissions provide a useful lens on the climate pressure associated with national production and energy systems.
caveat: The measure excludes land-use change and consumption embodied in trade and does not represent cumulative historical emissions.

name: Renewable energy consumption
definition: The share of total final energy consumption supplied by renewable sources, including modern renewables and traditional biomass.
interpretation: Higher shares can indicate cleaner energy, but high traditional biomass use may also reflect energy poverty and harmful household pollution.
whyItMatters: The energy mix affects emissions, air quality, energy security, industrial transition, and household wellbeing.
caveat: The aggregate does not distinguish modern clean renewables from unsustainable traditional biomass or show reliability and affordability.

name: Forest area
definition: The share of land under natural or planted stands of trees meeting the international forest definition.
interpretation: The value describes land cover rather than forest condition; trends and ecosystem context matter more than a universal ideal percentage.
whyItMatters: Forests support biodiversity, carbon storage, water cycles, livelihoods, cultural life, and resilience to hazards.
caveat: The measure does not distinguish primary forest from plantations, biodiversity quality, legal protection, degradation, or community rights.
